passage:
Dear Diary, Saturday
Last month, when I told Papa I cracked his phone screen, he shouted so the neighbours heard, and made me say "I am careless" in front of Dadi and my cousins. Everyone laughed. I cried in the bathroom.
So today, when I tore my uniform on the gate, I said a boy pushed me. Nobody pushed me. I just didn't want the shouting again. My hands shook the whole time.
Vasudha Masi found me crying on the stairs. I told her everything, even the lie. She said, "Keerthana, this is not your fault. Telling the truth should never feel this scary." Tonight she talked to Papa for a long time. He came and said sorry. I don't know yet if I believe him.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say had happened to the uniform?
qa.a: Keerthana said a boy pushed, though nobody pushed and the uniform tore on the gate.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana lie about the torn uniform?
qa.a: After being shouted at and made to say "I am careless" in front of family, Keerthana feared the same humiliation, so lying felt safer.

qa.q: What did Vasudha Masi do that helped?
qa.a: She listened to everything Keerthana told her, said it wasn't Keerthana's fault, and talked to Papa that same night.

qa.q: Why might Papa have come to say sorry after talking with Vasudha Masi?
qa.a: He may have realised that his shouting and mocking taught Keerthana that the truth was dangerous, which is why the lie happened.

grounding: A child humiliated for confessing learns that lying feels safer than the truth, until a trusted adult listens and speaks to the parent the same day.

passage:
In the village school, Vinita Ma'am had one rule for mistakes: whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period. One Monday morning Hafsa admitted forgetting her sums and stood there while the class giggled, ears burning.
After lunch Ma'am asked for the spelling homework. Hafsa had forgotten that too. She said, "I did it, Ma'am, but the goat ate the page." Her voice was steady. Inside she was shaking.
The new head teacher had seen Hafsa on the bench through the window that morning. That afternoon she called Hafsa in and said, "I think you were afraid of the bench. You won't be punished for the truth." Hafsa cried and told her. Before the bell, the head teacher spoke with Vinita Ma'am, and the bench rule ended that day.

qa.q: What was Vinita Ma'am's rule for mistakes?
qa.a: Whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa lie after lunch?
qa.a: She feared being humiliated on the bench again while the class giggled, so a lie felt safer than confessing.

qa.q: What did the head teacher do that helped?
qa.a: She called Hafsa in calmly, named the fear, promised no punishment for the truth, and spoke to Vinita Ma'am the same day to end the rule.

qa.q: How might the other children change after the bench rule ends?
qa.a: They may feel safer admitting mistakes, instead of learning, like Hafsa, that lying is safer than the truth.

grounding: A girl humiliated for confessing at school learns to lie, showing that fear of punishment teaches deception until an adult makes the truth safe.

passage:
The power went out in the middle of the Class 5 half-yearly exam, and the room went dim. In the confusion, Naveen knocked over his ink bottle. It splashed across the answer sheet of the boy next to him.
Siddharth Sir walked over with his torch. "Who spilled this?"
Naveen's mouth went dry. A month ago, when he had confessed to breaking the class globe, Siddharth Sir had made him stand on the bench for the whole period while the class laughed. He still remembered every face.
"I don't know, Sir," Naveen said. "It was dark."
His neighbour stared at him. Naveen stared at his paper. His hands were shaking.
He knew he was lying. He also knew, very clearly, that the truth had cost him more last time. That evening he told his mother everything, crying, and she said she would speak to the principal the next morning.

qa.q: What did Naveen knock over?
qa.a: He knocked over his ink bottle.

qa.q: Why did Naveen say "I don't know, Sir"?
qa.a: Naveen felt afraid of being humiliated again, because the last time he told the truth he was made to stand on the bench while the class laughed.

qa.q: What could make it safer for Naveen to tell the truth in class?
qa.a: If Sir responded to confessions calmly and privately instead of shaming, and with his mother and the principal involved, Naveen would learn truth is safe.

qa.q: How might Naveen's neighbour feel when Naveen says he doesn't know?
qa.a: The neighbour probably feels angry and unfairly treated, staring at Naveen because his answer sheet is ruined.

grounding: It shows a child who was humiliated for confessing now lying out of fear under pressure, learning that lying feels safer than truth.

passage:
Last month, when Nandini admitted she had left her tiffin box on the school bus, her mother put Mahima Masi on speakerphone at dinner and told the whole story. "Our careless donkey loses everything!" Everyone laughed. Nandini laughed too, then cried in the bathroom.
Now, on Saturday, Nandini was alone in the living room when Masi's reading glasses slid off the sofa and cracked under her foot.
Her heart pounded.
She pushed the glasses under the cushion.
When Masi asked, "Has anyone seen my glasses?", Nandini said, "No, Masi," and went to her room. She sat on her bed, feeling sick. It was that telling the truth had been worse.
Later that evening, Masi knocked gently and sat with her. "Whatever happened, I won't laugh. I promise." Nandini burst into tears and told her.

qa.q: What happened to Masi's reading glasses?
qa.a: They slid off the sofa and cracked under her foot.

qa.q: Why did Nandini hide the glasses?
qa.a: Nandini felt afraid of being humiliated again at dinner, since last time her honesty led to laughter and being called a donkey.

qa.q: What did Masi do that made the truth feel safe?
qa.a: Masi came to her privately, sat with her and promised not to laugh, so Nandini could tell her.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother feel if she understood why Nandini hid the glasses?
qa.a: She might feel sorry and a bit ashamed, realising the joke at dinner taught Nandini that truth brings humiliation.

grounding: It shows a child who was mocked for confessing learning to hide a mistake, until an adult makes the truth safe.

passage:
"Bidisha, why did you tell Baba your uniform tore on the bus door?" Harsha asked, sitting on the stairs of their building. "I saw you catch it on the gate while climbing."
Bidisha twisted the torn sleeve. "Because."
"Because what?"
"Last time I told Baba the truth about breaking the flowerpot, he made me go to every flat and say sorry. Everyone laughed. The aunties called me 'flowerpot' for weeks."
"That sounds horrible."
"So now I just say something else. It's easier."
Harsha was quiet. "Do you like lying?"
"No. My stomach hurts when I do."
"What if I come with you and we tell Baba together? I'll ask him not to make it a show."
Bidisha looked up. "Will he listen to you?"
"He listens to me. Come. And if he laughs, I'll tell him it isn't funny."

qa.q: How did Bidisha actually tear her uniform?
qa.a: Bidisha caught it on the gate while climbing.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha lie to Baba about the uniform?
qa.a: Bidisha felt afraid of being humiliated again, since last time the truth led to apologising at every flat and being mocked for weeks.

qa.q: How does Harsha offer to help?
qa.a: Harsha offers to go with Bidisha to tell Baba together and to ask him not to make it a show.

qa.q: How might Baba feel if he understood why Bidisha lied?
qa.a: Baba might feel regret, realising his public punishment taught Bidisha that lying is safer than truth.

grounding: It shows a child who was humiliated for confessing now lying out of fear, and a cousin offering to make the truth safe.

passage:
I'm Nirmala. Last year I broke Papa's reading glasses by mistake, and I told him straight away. He shouted so loudly the neighbours came out, and he made me stand outside the door holding the broken glasses while everyone looked.
So when I tore my school sweater, I said a dog did it. When Ojas, my little brother, spilled ink on the register, I told him to say it was already there. Lying felt safer.
Then my teacher, Mrs Dsouza, asked me why I always said "not me" so fast. I told her about the glasses. She looked sad. She said, "Nobody should be shamed for telling the truth." That same afternoon she called Mummy in, and they talked for a long time.
Mummy has started saying, "Thank you for telling me." I'm trying to believe her.

qa.q: What did Nirmala break last year?
qa.a: Papa's reading glasses, by mistake.

qa.q: Why did lying start to feel safer to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and afraid after being shouted at and made to stand outside for telling the truth, so lying seemed safer.

qa.q: What did Mrs Dsouza do the same day?
qa.a: She listened, said nobody should be shamed for telling the truth, and called Mummy in that afternoon to talk.

qa.q: What is Ojas learning from this?
qa.a: Ojas, told to say the ink was already there, is learning that lying protects you, the same lesson Nirmala learnt from being humiliated.

grounding: Shows a child humiliated for confessing learning that lying feels safer, and a teacher acting the same day to make the truth safe again.
